messages.content: Explain in exactly three sentences why floating-point addition is not associative.
Explain in exactly three sentences why floating-point addition is not associative.

samples.text: Floating‑point numbers have a finite mantissa, so each arithmetic operation rounds the exact real result to the nearest representable value. When you add three numbers, the intermediate rounding after the first addition can change the magnitude and exponent of the partial sum, causing a different rounding error than if you add the other two first. Consequently, (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) can produce distinct floating‑point results, breaking associativity.

Floating‑point numbers have a finite precision, so each operation rounds the exact real result to the nearest representable value. When you add three numbers, rounding after the first addition can change the magnitude of the intermediate sum, causing a different rounding error than if you round after the second addition. Consequently, (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) can produce different floating‑point results, breaking associativity.

Floating‑point numbers have a finite precision, so each arithmetic operation rounds the exact real result to the nearest representable value. Because the rounding is performed after every addition, the intermediate value produced by \((a+b)+c\) can differ from the one produced by \(a+(b+c)\) when the rounding errors accumulate in different ways. Consequently, the two possible evaluation orders can yield distinct floating‑point results, breaking the associativity property of addition.

Thus the rounding errors introduced at different steps break the mathematical associativity of addition in floating‑point arithmetic.

Because rounding is performed after every addition, the intermediate rounding error depends on which pair of numbers is added first, causing the final rounded sum to differ for \((a+b)+c\) versus \(a+(b+c)\). Thus the limited precision and per‑operation rounding break the mathematical associativity property for floating‑point addition.
